warmup.text: Last day of the unit. Today's poem imagines a Native speaker, but a white poet wrote it. Set it beside the letter a Choctaw chief wrote for himself, and ask which one you would trust, and for what.

words.text: One last time: say why the exact word matters when you write about history. Keep the novel and the record apart in every sentence. Then open the last three ears of corn.

reading.text: Reread the two sources, then look back through Chapters 28 and 29. Choose one moment from the novel and one line from a source to set side by side. Then try the Read Like a Writer box on your own.

assignment.text: Write your claim, then your final source comparison paragraph, formal and complete. Last, tell what a story told by a ghost taught you about real history. Copy your work and paste it into Canvas.

readnow.text: Reread the two sources on this page. Then look back at Chapters 28 and 29 in your book.

do: Tap the highlighted words in the first sentence.
Say the second one in formal style, out loud.
Tap Check My Work.
how.why: An essay about history uses exact words and names its sources.

do: Read the poem out loud once.
Read who wrote it, and when.
Read Think About It and keep your answer in mind.
how.why: A poem written at the time is a primary source. It shows what someone thought back then.

do: Read why the exact word matters.
Tap a word, then tap its meaning.
Match all four.
how.why: The word you choose for an event is part of your argument about it.

do: Read each word and its meaning.
Write one sentence for each word.
Make each sentence show the meaning.
how.why: Using a word in your own sentence is the best proof you know it.

do: Read the blurred and the distinct sentence.
Tap the version that keeps the novel and the record apart.
Explain the problem in the box, with one blurred and one fixed sentence.
how.why: A reader must always know what is made up and what is on the record.

do: Ask what job each word does.
Tap a word.
Then tap noun, verb or adjective.
how.why: The ending of a long word tells you its job in the sentence.

do: Read the three lenses.
Tap the one you will use today.
Say what the novel is for and what the sources are for.
how.why: Synthesizing means putting the pieces together into one big idea.
how.use: You will use this in your final paragraph.

do: Reread Source A.
Reread Source B.
Choose the line you will quote.
how.why: Your paragraph needs the exact words of one real source.

do: Look back at Chapters 28 and 29 and the two sources.
Answer each question in 2 or more sentences.
For question 1, write only your claim and name your two pieces of evidence.
how.why: These questions check what happened and what the author shows you.

do: Write the final paragraph in the box.
Check: claim, evidence from the novel, evidence from a source, reasoning.
Add what this ghost story taught you about history.
how.why: Today you finish your comparison and turn it in.

do: Read what courage means.
Read the example from this week.
After you read, pick the strongest moment of the week at the end of this tab.
Read the introduction below.
Reread the two sources. Then look back at Chapters 28 and 29.
Then do the Read Like a Writer box and the Virtue Watch below.

glossary.meaning: put ideas together to make one bigger idea
a nation's right to govern itself

miss.contradict: It names an action: to say the opposite. A verb.
miss.displacement: It ends in -ment, so it names a thing. A noun.
miss.federal: It ends in -al and describes, as in federal law. An adjective.
miss.historical: It ends in -al and describes, as in historical record. An adjective.
miss.negotiate: It ends in -ate and names an action. A verb.
miss.primary: It describes, as in primary source. An adjective.
miss.sovereignty: It ends in -ty, so it names a thing. A noun.
miss.testify: It ends in -ify and names an action. A verb.
miss.testimony: It names a thing: what a witness says. A noun.

game.title: Ears of Corn
game.sub: This week's word game · 3 words today
game.look: Each long word is an ear of corn, like the corn the families cook in Chapter 29. The parts added to the front or the end are the husks. Tap each husk to peel it away. The base word is the ear inside.

do: Read the long word.
Find the part that can stand alone as a word. Leave it.
Tap each part added to the front or the end.
Tap Next word.
how.why: Long words in history writing are short words with parts added. Find the base and you can read and spell the rest.

game.doneLine: Every ear this week is open. Well done.

ears.why: un- means not. This word has three husks: one at the front and two at the end.
-ful means full of, and -ness makes a noun.
ears.means: the habit of telling the truth.

ears.why: re- means again, and here -al makes a noun.

art.title: Mó-sho-la-túb-bee, a Choctaw chief
art.alt: A painted portrait of a seated man in a blue-green patterned coat with a red sash, holding a feather fan and a long pipe.
art.look: George Catlin painted this Choctaw chief in 1834, in Indian Territory, west of the Mississippi River. He was one of the leaders who signed the Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek in 1830. Four years later, after the removal, he sat for this portrait in the West. The Choctaw Nation is still there today, in Oklahoma.
